items.title: Plain English: replacing wordy phrases (Level 2)
items.source: GOV.UK Style Guide; GOV.UK content design guidance
items.body: Plain English works on whole phrases as well as single words. Many phrases are padding that can be replaced by one or two short words. 'At this point in time' becomes 'now'. 'Due to the fact that' becomes 'because'. 'In order to' becomes 'to'. 'With regard to' becomes 'about'. 'In the near future' becomes 'soon'. 'Is able to' becomes 'can'. 'A number of' becomes 'several' or 'some'. Watch for verbs that have been turned into nouns. 'Make a decision' is just 'decide', 'give consideration to' is 'consider', 'make an application' is 'apply' and 'provide assistance' is 'help'. Old-fashioned openings such as 'Please find attached herewith' are better as 'I have attached'. Government writing often drifts into vague management jargon, such as 'going forward', 'stakeholders', 'leverage' and 'robust'. GOV.UK guidance advises against words like these because they hide the real meaning. If a sentence says 'we will engage stakeholders', ask yourself who exactly, and how. Name the people, say what will happen and say when. Use 'people' rather than 'individuals' or 'persons', and 'live' rather than 'reside'. Plain English helps expert readers too. Experts are often short of time and prefer a message they can understand at one reading.

questions.prompt: Which single word can replace 'due to the fact that' without changing the meaning?

options.text: although
because
unless
whereas

questions.hint: 'Because' says the same as 'due to the fact that' in one word.

questions.prompt: Which sentence says 'We need your proof of address in order to process your claim' most plainly?

options.text: We need your proof of address to process your claim.
We need your proof of address for the purpose of claim processing.
We need your proof of address with a view to processing your claim.
We need your proof of address so as to enable claim processing.

questions.hint: 'In order to' can nearly always be shortened to 'to'.

questions.prompt: Which phrase is plainer than 'a number of'?

options.text: an assortment of
a multitude of
several
a quantity of

questions.hint: 'Several' or 'some' is plainer than 'a number of'.

questions.prompt: In plain English, what does 'give consideration to' become?

options.text: consider
take a view about
have regard for
pay attention toward

questions.hint: Turning the noun back into a verb removes the padding.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the plainest way to introduce an attachment?

options.text: I have attached the form you asked for.
Please find attached herewith the form you asked for.
Attached hereto is the form that you requested of us.
The form you asked for is enclosed for your attention.

questions.hint: Old-fashioned phrases such as 'find attached herewith' should be avoided.

questions.prompt: A draft says 'We will engage stakeholders going forward.' What is the main problem?

options.text: It uses a Latin abbreviation
It is written in the passive voice
It uses vague jargon that does not say who or when
It is longer than 25 words

questions.hint: Jargon like 'stakeholders' and 'going forward' hides the real meaning.

questions.prompt: A letter says 'Individuals who reside in the area may apply.' Which is the plainest rewrite?

options.text: Persons who reside in the area can apply.
People residing in the area may apply.
Individuals who live in the area may apply.
People who live in the area can apply.

questions.hint: Use 'people' and 'live', and 'can' for 'may' where you mean ability.

questions.prompt: Which opening gets to the point fastest?

options.text: Following a review of your case, a decision has now been made.
Your parking permit has been approved.
Further to your recent letter, I am pleased to confirm the decision.
I am writing with regard to your recent application for a permit.

questions.hint: A good opening puts the main point in the first words.

questions.prompt: Why should you still use plain English when writing to experts?

options.text: Experts cannot understand technical language
Experts are short of time and prefer to understand at one reading
Experts need shorter documents than the public
Plain English is required by law in every government letter

questions.hint: Plain English saves every reader time, including specialists.

items.title: Structuring a message so it is easy to follow (Level 2)
items.source: GOV.UK Style Guide; GOV.UK content design guidance
items.body: Readers often skim, so the structure of a message matters as much as the words. Use the 'main point first' approach, sometimes called the inverted pyramid. Start with the most important information, such as the decision, the request or the deadline, and then give the background. Each message should have one main purpose. If you need to cover two unrelated things, send two messages. Use a heading for each section of a long document and make the headings tell the reader what they will find, for example 'What you need to do'. Use a numbered list when steps must be followed in order, such as the stages of making a claim. Use a bulleted list when the items have no order, such as documents a person may bring. Introduce a list with a lead-in line that ends in a colon, and make each point read naturally after that line. Use bold only for the odd word that really matters. If everything is bold, nothing stands out. When someone asks you several questions, answer them in the order they were asked, so that they can find each answer. Always say clearly what you want the reader to do and by when.

questions.prompt: What does the 'main point first' approach mean?

options.text: Start with thanks and finish with the main point
Start with a summary of the person's earlier letters
Start with the most important information, then add the background
Start with the background so the decision makes sense

questions.hint: Putting the main point first helps readers who skim.

questions.prompt: Which list type should you use for steps that must be followed in order?

options.text: A table with no headings
A paragraph of bold text
A bulleted list
A numbered list

questions.hint: Numbers show the sequence.

questions.prompt: Which list type suits documents a person may bring, in no particular order?

options.text: A list inside a table
A bulleted list
A numbered list
A list in alphabetical order

questions.hint: Bullets are used when order does not matter.

questions.prompt: How should a lead-in line before a bulleted list end?

options.text: With a colon
With a question mark
With a dash
With a full stop

questions.hint: A colon leads the reader into the list.

questions.prompt: Why does one message usually need only one main purpose?

options.text: A second topic should always be left for the next letter
A longer message must always be checked by a manager
Messages with two topics are blocked by email systems
The reader can see what to do and is less likely to miss a request

questions.hint: Separate messages make each request easy to spot.

questions.prompt: Which heading in a long document is most helpful to the reader?

options.text: What you need to do
Further information relating to the matter
Section 4
Additional matters

questions.hint: A clear heading tells the reader what the section contains.

questions.prompt: Why should bold be used sparingly?

options.text: Bold text takes more ink to print
If lots of text is bold, nothing stands out
Bold text cannot be read by screen readers
Bold is only allowed in the first paragraph

questions.hint: Emphasis works only when it is rare.

questions.prompt: A customer asks three questions in one email. How should you reply?

options.text: Answer the easiest question and say the others will follow
Send three separate replies on different days
Combine the answers into one general paragraph
Answer each question in the order they were asked

questions.hint: Following their order lets the customer find each answer.

questions.prompt: Which draft is better organised?

options.text: Following the review process, we can confirm that, subject to checks, a payment will be made on 4 July.
Thank you for your claim. Many claims arrive each week. Yours has now been looked at, and a payment of £120 is due.
We have looked at the information from your recent claim and its supporting evidence. A decision has been taken. Your claim is approved.
Your claim is approved. We will pay £120 on 4 July. You do not need to do anything.

questions.hint: The first draft gives the decision, the payment and the action first.

items.title: Accessible writing and punctuation (Level 2)
items.source: GOV.UK Style Guide; GOV.UK accessibility guidance for content
items.body: Accessible writing means that as many people as possible can read and use what you produce, including people with dyslexia, sight loss or learning disabilities, and people using screen readers. Align text to the left rather than justifying it, because justified text leaves uneven gaps between words that are hard to follow. Do not use colour as the only way to show meaning, because some people cannot tell colours apart. Add alternative text, called alt text, to an image so that a screen reader can describe it to someone who cannot see it. Do not underline words for emphasis, because underlining looks like a link. Avoid long stretches of capital letters or italics. Screen readers may spell out capitalised words letter by letter. Write 'and' instead of an ampersand. Easy Read is a format for people with learning disabilities that uses short sentences, plain words and supporting images. Use clear headings, because they help people to find the part they need. Some punctuation rules cause common mistakes. 'Its' without an apostrophe shows possession, as in 'the department sent its reply'. 'It's' with an apostrophe means 'it is' or 'it has'. An apostrophe before the s shows one owner ('the customer's letter'). After the s it shows more than one ('the customers' letters').

questions.prompt: Which word completes the sentence correctly? 'The department sent ___ reply on Monday.'

options.text: it's
its'
it is'
its

questions.hint: 'Its' without an apostrophe shows possession.

questions.prompt: Which phrase refers to the letter belonging to one customer?

options.text: the customer's letter
the customers letter
the customer letter's
the customers' letter

questions.hint: An apostrophe before the s shows one owner.

questions.prompt: Why is left-aligned text better than justified text for most readers?

options.text: Left-aligned text always fits many more words on each page
Justified text cannot be saved in some of the common file formats
Justified text is only allowed in formal letters, not on websites
Justified text creates uneven gaps between words that are hard to follow

questions.hint: Even spacing makes reading easier.

questions.prompt: What is alt text used for?

options.text: To describe an image to someone using a screen reader
To compress the image so it loads faster
To show who took the photograph
To give the image a title for the printed version

questions.hint: Alt text lets people who cannot see an image understand it.

questions.prompt: Why should you not use colour as the only way to show meaning?

options.text: Some readers cannot tell the colours apart
Coloured text is not allowed on GOV.UK
Colours print too lightly to see
Colours slow down web pages

questions.hint: People with colour blindness may miss the meaning.

questions.prompt: Why should you avoid underlining a word for emphasis in a web page?

options.text: It is only used for headings
It makes the word harder to spell
It looks like a link
It cannot be printed

questions.hint: Underlined text is read as a link by users.

questions.prompt: What is Easy Read, as a format for writing?

options.text: A training method that helps busy staff to read long reports quickly
A format with short sentences, plain words and images for people with learning disabilities
A short summary of any long document, printed in large type for slow readers
A software tool that rewrites a document in simple language automatically

questions.hint: Easy Read supports understanding with simple words and pictures.

questions.prompt: Why are long sections in capital letters a problem for screen readers?

options.text: They are read twice as fast
They may be read out letter by letter
They are translated into another language
They are skipped completely

questions.hint: Screen readers can treat capitalised words as initials.

items.title: Emails: subject lines and openings (Level 2)
items.source: GOV.UK content design guidance; ICO guidance on personal data
items.body: The subject line is the first thing a reader sees, and on a phone it may be cut short, so keep it brief and put the key words first. A good subject line says what the email is about and, where needed, what the reader must do and by when: 'Confirm your address by 8 July'. Vague subjects such as 'Query' or 'Update' help nobody. Do not put personal data in a subject line. Subject lines can be seen in notifications and previews, and are copied into logs, so a name with a National Insurance number or a health detail should stay inside the secure body of the message, if it needs to be sent by email at all. Use the reference number if you have one. If a long email chain moves on to a new subject, change the subject line or start a new email, so that people searching later can find it. Labels such as 'FYI' (for your information) and 'Action needed' help colleagues sort their inbox, but do not overuse 'Urgent'. Open with the reason you are writing in the first sentence. Skip filler such as 'I hope this email finds you well' when writing to busy members of the public. If you are replying, refer to what they sent, for example 'Thank you for your email of 5 June about your payment'.

questions.prompt: Which subject line best asks a customer to confirm their address by 8 July?

options.text: Important update about your case
Information about your account
Your recent query: please reply
Confirm your address by 8 July

questions.hint: A good subject line states the action and the deadline.

questions.prompt: Which of these should NOT appear in an email subject line?

options.text: The name of the service
A customer's National Insurance number
The deadline for a reply
A case reference number

questions.hint: Personal data should not appear in subject lines, where it can be seen in previews.

questions.prompt: What does 'FYI' stand for in an email subject line?

options.text: For your information
Follow your instructions
File your invoice
For yesterday's issue

questions.hint: FYI tells the reader no action is needed.

questions.prompt: Why should the key words come first in a subject line?

options.text: Long subject lines can be cut off on phones
Email systems sort alphabetically by the first word
Subject lines must be under 10 characters
Readers only open emails marked urgent

questions.hint: Cut-off subjects hide the end of the line.

questions.prompt: A long email chain about a payment now covers a new issue. What should you do?

options.text: Delete the earlier messages
Copy in your manager before replying
Change the subject line or start a new email
Leave the subject unchanged to keep one chain

questions.hint: A new subject helps people to find the message later.

questions.prompt: Which opening line is most suitable for a busy member of the public?

options.text: Many thanks for taking the time to contact us today.
I am writing in response to your recent communication to our office.
I hope this email finds you well and that you are having a good week.
Thank you for your email of 5 June about your payment.

questions.hint: A good opening refers to what they sent and gets to the point.

questions.prompt: Why should the word 'Urgent' be used sparingly?

options.text: If it is overused, readers stop treating it as a signal
It delays delivery of the message
It is on a list of words banned from government emails
It makes the email take longer to reach staff

questions.hint: Overuse makes urgent messages harder to spot.

questions.prompt: Which subject line is the vaguest?

options.text: Reference 4471: change to your appointment
Your housing benefit claim: documents needed
Query
Your appointment on Tuesday 4 March

questions.hint: A one-word subject does not tell the reader what the email is about.

items.title: Emails: attachments, tone and replies (Level 2)
items.source: GOV.UK content design guidance; Freedom of Information Act 2000
items.body: Good email habits save time and protect the organisation. Mention any attachment in the body of the message so the reader knows what it is and why you have sent it, and check that it is actually attached. Give files clear names, such as 'Housing-benefit-claim-form.pdf', not 'scan0001.pdf', and think about the file size, because very large files may be blocked. Keep your tone polite and calm. If a customer's email is angry, take a moment before replying, deal with the problem rather than the tone, and apologise sincerely where the department has made a mistake. Avoid phrases such as 'As I said before' and 'Unfortunately you have failed to'. If you cannot give a full answer straight away, acknowledge the email and say when you will reply. Remember that emails are records. They can be released under the Freedom of Information Act 2000, or in response to a data subject access request, so write nothing you would not be happy to see published. Before you forward a long chain, scroll down and check the older messages for personal data or comments that the new reader should not see. An out-of-office message should give the dates you are away and a colleague to contact, but not the reason you are away or personal details.

questions.prompt: Why should you mention an attachment in the body of an email?

options.text: So that the attachment can be opened without a password
So the reader knows what it is and why it has been sent
So that the email avoids being blocked by security systems
So that the file is copied to the department's archive

questions.hint: Telling the reader what the attachment is helps them use it.

questions.prompt: Which file name is the most helpful?

options.text: Housing-benefit-claim-form.pdf
document_for_review.pdf
final_version_new2_checked.pdf
scan0001_copy_final.pdf

questions.hint: A descriptive name says what the file is.

questions.prompt: What should an out-of-office message NOT include?

options.text: A short, polite greeting
The date you will return
The personal reason you are away
The name of a colleague to contact

questions.hint: Reasons for absence are personal and should not be shared.

questions.prompt: Which reply best handles a customer who is annoyed about a late payment?

options.text: Delays happen to many people, so this is not unusual. Payment will be made soon.
I'm sorry your payment is late. I have checked, and it will reach you by Friday.
As already explained, payments take time. Please be patient.
Your complaint has been noted. We apologise for any inconvenience caused.

questions.hint: A good reply apologises, explains and gives a clear next step.

questions.prompt: Why should you write emails as though they could be made public?

options.text: Customers are sent copies of all internal emails
Managers read all emails sent by new staff
They are all published on GOV.UK after a year
They can be released under the Freedom of Information Act 2000

questions.hint: Emails are records and may be disclosed.

questions.prompt: You cannot fully answer a customer's email today. What should you do?

options.text: Forward it to a colleague without telling the customer
Wait until you have the full answer before replying
Reply to say the question cannot be answered
Acknowledge it and say when you will reply

questions.hint: An acknowledgement manages the customer's expectations.

questions.prompt: What should you check before forwarding a long email chain?

options.text: That all earlier messages are in the same font
That the chain is less than 24 hours old
That the subject line has the word 'Fwd'
Older messages for personal data the new reader should not see

questions.hint: Older messages in a chain may contain information not meant for the new recipient.

questions.prompt: Which phrase is likely to annoy a customer who has written to you?

options.text: I understand how frustrating this is
I have checked your record
Thank you for your patience
As I said before

questions.hint: Phrases that blame the reader create a poor tone.

items.title: Letters to the public: acknowledging, refusing and apologising (Level 2)
items.source: GOV.UK content design guidance; Civil Service Code
items.body: Different letters have different jobs. An acknowledgement letter confirms that you have received something and tells the person what will happen next and when. A request-for-information letter lists exactly what you need, in a bulleted list, with a deadline and where to send it. A decision letter states the decision in the first line. If the decision is a refusal, the letter must explain the reason in plain words and tell the person how to challenge it, for example how to ask for a review or appeal and how long they have to do so. Do not hide bad news at the end. Say it early, kindly and clearly. An apology letter should say sorry, explain briefly what went wrong, and say what you will do to put it right. One sincere apology is better than several. Do not blame other people or give long excuses. Do not promise anything you cannot be sure of, such as an exact payment date, unless you know it will be met. Give a named contact and a direct number if you can, because people are happier dealing with a person than a general address. If you send documents with the letter, list them after your name with 'Enc.' (enclosures), so the reader can check nothing is missing.

questions.prompt: What is the main job of an acknowledgement letter?

options.text: To ask the person for further evidence
To apologise for the department's delay
To give the final decision on a case
To confirm receipt and say what will happen next and when

questions.hint: An acknowledgement tells people their letter arrived and what to expect.

questions.prompt: What must a refusal letter explain besides the decision?

options.text: The names of the officers who made the decision
The department's budget for the year
The history of the policy behind the decision
The reason and how to ask for a review or appeal

questions.hint: People need to understand why and know how to challenge the decision.

questions.prompt: Where should bad news go in a letter?

options.text: At the very end, after the contact details
Hidden in the middle of a long paragraph
In a separate leaflet that is sent later
Near the start, said clearly and kindly

questions.hint: Do not make readers hunt for the decision.

questions.prompt: Which is the best structure for an apology?

options.text: Say sorry, explain what went wrong, say what you will do
Say sorry several times and promise it will not happen again
Say sorry only if the person has complained twice
Explain the cause at length, then say sorry once

questions.hint: A sincere apology is brief and followed by action.

questions.prompt: Which statement should you avoid making in a letter?

options.text: We guarantee you will be paid next week
We will write again by 30 June
We aim to pay you within 10 working days
We have received your form

questions.hint: Do not promise outcomes that you cannot be sure of.

questions.prompt: What does 'Enc.' at the bottom of a letter mean?

options.text: The letter has been encoded for security
The letter is encrypted
The letter is a final notice
Documents are enclosed with the letter

questions.hint: 'Enc.' lists the enclosures sent with the letter.

questions.prompt: Why give a named contact in a letter?

options.text: It removes the need for a reference number
People prefer dealing with a person rather than a general address
The letter can then be shorter
The named person can be blamed for errors

questions.hint: A named contact makes help easier to get.

questions.prompt: Which bad-news sentence is the clearest and kindest?

options.text: We regret that, on this occasion, your circumstances do not meet the criteria set for this payment, so we cannot help.
Your claim has not been successful for the reasons outlined in the relevant guidance, which is available on request.
We cannot pay you this month because we did not receive your form by 3 May. You can ask us to look again by writing before 1 June.
Unfortunately you have failed to send your form on time and so no payment can be made this month under the guidance.

questions.hint: A clear reason and a route to challenge make the sentence helpful.

items.title: Spreadsheets: order of operations and percentages (Level 2)
items.source: Microsoft Excel help; Google Sheets help
items.body: A spreadsheet follows the usual order of operations, often remembered as BODMAS. Brackets come first, then orders (powers), then division and multiplication, and then addition and subtraction. So =2+3*4 gives 14, because the multiplication happens first, while =(2+3)*4 gives 20 because the brackets are worked out first. The symbol for a power is ^, so =3^2 gives 9. To find a percentage of a number, multiply by the percentage. =50*20% gives 10, and =50*0.2 gives the same. To add VAT at 20%, multiply the price by 1.2, so £80 becomes £96. Percentage change is the difference divided by the original: (new - old) / old. From 40 to 50 the change is (50-40)/40 = 0.25, which you format as a percentage to show 25%. Percentage format multiplies the stored value by 100 for display only. The number 0.075 shows as 7.5%. If you type 15% into a cell, the spreadsheet stores 0.15. Formatting does not change the underlying number, so a cell showing 20% still holds 0.2 and calculations use 0.2.

questions.prompt: A cell holds =2+3*4. What number does it display?
questions.hint: Multiplication is done before addition, so 3*4 = 12 and 12+2 = 14.

questions.prompt: Brackets are added to give =(2+3)*4. What is the result now?
questions.hint: Brackets are worked out first, so 5*4 = 20.

questions.prompt: What does =10-4/2 return?
questions.hint: Division comes first: 4/2 = 2, then 10-2 = 8.

questions.prompt: What value does the formula =2*3^2 give?
questions.hint: The power is done first: 3^2 = 9, then 2*9 = 18.

questions.prompt: What does =50*20% return?
A price of £80 needs 20% VAT added. Which formula gives the total price?
questions.hint: Multiplying by 1.2 adds 20% to the price, giving £96.

questions.prompt: A figure rises from 40 to 50. What is the percentage increase?
A cell holds 0.075 and has percentage format. What does it display?
questions.hint: Percentage format multiplies by 100 for display.

questions.prompt: If you type 15% into a cell, what number is stored?
questions.hint: A percentage is stored as a decimal fraction.

items.title: Spreadsheets: counting, rounding and copying formulas (Level 2)
items.source: Microsoft Excel help; Google Sheets help
items.body: COUNT counts only cells that contain numbers. COUNTA counts every cell that is not empty, including text. COUNTBLANK counts empty cells. Suppose A1:A5 holds 3, 7, the text n/a, an empty cell and 5. Then COUNT gives 3, COUNTA gives 4, COUNTBLANK gives 1, SUM gives 15 and AVERAGE gives 5, because SUM and AVERAGE ignore text and blanks. Note that AVERAGE divides 15 by 3, not by 5. ROUND(number, digits) rounds a number. =ROUND(3.14159,2) gives 3.14 and =ROUND(2.5,0) gives 3. ROUNDUP and ROUNDDOWN always go away from or towards zero. Rounding in a formula changes the value, whereas formatting only changes how it looks. The fill handle is the small square at the corner of a selected cell. Dragging it copies a formula to nearby cells. By default references are relative, so they move with the formula. If =A1+B1 is in row 1 and you copy it down one row, it becomes =A2+B2. Numbers are normally aligned to the right of a cell and text to the left. A number stored as text, often shown with a green triangle in Excel, is not added by SUM. The error #DIV/0! appears when a formula divides by zero or by an empty cell.

questions.prompt: A1:A5 holds 3, 7, the text n/a, an empty cell and 5. What does COUNT give?
questions.hint: COUNT only counts the cells that hold numbers.

questions.prompt: Using that same range, how many cells does COUNTA count?
questions.hint: COUNTA counts every non-empty cell, including the text.

questions.prompt: What mean does AVERAGE give for that range?
questions.hint: AVERAGE uses only the three numbers: 15 divided by 3 is 5.

questions.prompt: How many empty cells does COUNTBLANK find in that range?
questions.hint: There is one empty cell in the range.

questions.prompt: What does =ROUND(3.14159,2) return?
questions.hint: Rounding to two decimal places gives 3.14.

questions.prompt: What does =ROUND(2.5,0) return?
questions.hint: Spreadsheets round halves away from zero, so 2.5 becomes 3.

questions.prompt: The formula =A1+B1 sits in row 1. What is it after being copied down one row?
questions.hint: Relative references move with the formula.

questions.prompt: A number typed as text is in a cell. What happens when SUM includes it?

options.text: SUM turns the whole total into text
SUM ignores it
SUM treats it as zero and shows an error
SUM adds it as normal

questions.hint: Numbers stored as text are not added by SUM.

questions.prompt: What causes the error #DIV/0!?

options.text: A number is too wide for the column
Dividing by zero or by an empty cell
A function name is spelt wrongly
A cell reference points to a deleted cell

questions.hint: The formula tried to divide by zero.

questions.prompt: What is the small square at the corner of a selected cell, used for copying formulas, called?

options.text: The formula bar
The fill handle
The name box
The range selector

questions.hint: Dragging the fill handle copies a formula or series.

items.title: Spreadsheets: keeping data tidy for sorting and filtering (Level 2)
items.source: Microsoft Excel help; Google Sheets help
items.body: Sorting and filtering only work well when data is tidy. Click inside the table, or select the whole table, before you sort. If you sort only one column, the other columns stay where they are, and names no longer match their figures. You can sort by more than one level, for example by Department first and then by Name within each department. Filters can be set by condition: a number filter such as 'greater than 50' shows only rows above 50, and a text filter can show cells that contain a word. Inconsistent entries cause problems. If staff are recorded as 'HR', 'H.R.' and 'Human Resources', a filter treats them as three different values. Extra spaces cause the same trouble. Merged cells make sorting and filtering difficult, so avoid them inside a table. Remove Duplicates deletes repeated rows. Data validation limits what can be entered into a cell, such as a drop-down list of allowed departments, which keeps entries consistent. A CSV file is a plain text file where values are separated by commas. It stores no formulas or formatting, and most systems can import one. Excel stores dates as numbers, counting days from a start date, and the format decides how they are displayed. This is why a date can sometimes show as a five-digit number.

questions.prompt: You sort only column A of a table with names in A and salaries in B. What goes wrong?

options.text: The salaries are deleted
The sort is blocked with an error
Names no longer match their salaries
The names are changed to capitals

questions.hint: Sorting one column on its own separates it from the other data.

questions.prompt: How do you sort staff by Department and then by Name within each department?

options.text: Use Remove Duplicates
Use a sort with more than one level
Filter by Department then delete the rest
Sort by Name twice

questions.hint: A multi-level sort orders by one column then another.

questions.prompt: What does a number filter set to 'greater than 50' show?

options.text: Only rows with exactly 50
Only rows with values above 50
Only rows with values of 50 or below
All rows, with values over 50 in bold

questions.hint: The filter keeps matching rows and hides the others.

questions.prompt: Why might a filter treat 'HR' and 'Human Resources' as separate departments?

options.text: Filters only work on capital letters
The words are in different columns
They are different entries, even though they mean the same
Filters ignore text longer than two words

questions.hint: Filters match entries exactly, so inconsistent wording splits the data.

questions.prompt: What does the Remove Duplicates tool do?

options.text: Hides rows with no data
Merges similar rows into one cell
Deletes repeated rows
Sorts the list alphabetically

questions.hint: It deletes rows that repeat the same values.

options.text: Plain text with values separated by commas
An image of the spreadsheet
Only the formatting of the sheet
A full workbook with formulas and charts

questions.hint: CSV files store values only, with no formulas or formatting.

questions.prompt: What does data validation do?

options.text: Checks that the numbers add up correctly
Changes text into numbers
Locks the sheet so nobody can read it
Limits what can be entered, such as a drop-down list

questions.hint: Validation keeps entries consistent.

questions.prompt: Why can a date appear as a five-digit number?

options.text: Dates are stored as numbers and the cell is not formatted as a date
The cell contains a formula error
The date is too old for the spreadsheet
The file has been saved as a CSV

questions.hint: The number is the stored date value, and a date format would display it.

items.title: Security classifications in practice (Level 2)
items.source: Government Security Classifications Policy; HMG Personnel Security Controls
items.body: The person who creates or owns a piece of information, called the originator, normally decides its classification by asking how much harm there would be if it were lost, stolen or seen by the wrong person. Most information is OFFICIAL and needs only baseline protection, such as locked buildings, passwords and sensible handling. Staff handling OFFICIAL information normally have a basic check called the Baseline Personnel Security Standard (BPSS). Access to SECRET information usually needs Security Check (SC) clearance, and regular access to TOP SECRET information needs Developed Vetting (DV). Information marked OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE needs extra care, for example a list of staff home addresses or commercially sensitive contract details. Do not discuss it in public places such as trains or cafes. Collect printouts from the printer straight away. Do not send work information to or from personal email accounts, and use only approved devices and systems, including when working from home. Combining a lot of OFFICIAL records can make the whole collection more sensitive. This is called aggregation. Always ask your manager or security team if you are unsure how to handle something. Higher classifications need classification markings at the top and bottom of each page, and stricter rules for storage, movement and destruction.

questions.prompt: Who normally decides the classification of a piece of information?

options.text: The Cabinet Secretary
The originator, who creates or owns it
The person who receives it first
The department's press office

questions.hint: The originator assesses how much harm its loss would cause.

questions.prompt: How much protection does OFFICIAL information typically need?

options.text: Nothing at all, because it is not secret
Storage in a safe at all times
Encryption and a security guard for every document
Baseline controls such as passwords and locked buildings

questions.hint: OFFICIAL needs sensible, baseline protection.

questions.prompt: Which clearance level normally allows regular access to SECRET information?

options.text: Developed Vetting (DV)
Baseline Personnel Security Standard (BPSS)
Security Check (SC)
Counter-Terrorist Check only

questions.hint: SC is the usual level for SECRET material.

questions.prompt: Which vetting level is normally needed for regular access to TOP SECRET information?

options.text: A standard reference check
Baseline Personnel Security Standard (BPSS)
Developed Vetting (DV)
Security Check (SC)

questions.hint: DV is the most thorough level.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a likely reason to mark a list OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE?

options.text: It lists the department's opening hours
It is a published press release
It contains staff home addresses
It lists public holiday dates

questions.hint: Personal data about staff needs extra care.

questions.prompt: A colleague wants to discuss an OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE case loudly on a train. What should you do?

options.text: Whisper the names only
Discuss it, but avoid mentioning the department
Suggest waiting until you are somewhere private
Join in, as the train is quiet

questions.hint: Sensitive details should not be discussed in public places.

options.text: Personal email is slower than work email
Personal accounts are not approved systems for government information
The attachment may be too big
The document may lose its formatting

questions.hint: Only approved systems and devices should be used.

questions.prompt: What does 'aggregation' mean when classifying information?

options.text: Sharing one record with several teams
Deleting old records to save space
Combining many records can make the whole collection more sensitive
Sending several documents at once

questions.hint: A large set of records may be more sensitive than one record.

items.title: UK GDPR: principles, lawful bases and rights (Level 2)
items.source: ICO guidance on the UK GDPR
items.body: The UK GDPR sets out seven principles for handling personal data: lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality (security); and accountability. Purpose limitation means you collect data for a stated purpose and do not use it for something incompatible. Storage limitation means you do not keep data longer than you need it. Integrity and confidentiality means you keep it secure. Accountability means you must be able to show that you follow the rules. To use personal data you need a lawful basis. There are six: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task and legitimate interests. Government departments mostly rely on public task or legal obligation. A privacy notice tells people what data is collected, why, how long it is kept and what their rights are. Individuals have rights, including access to their data, correction of inaccurate data (rectification), erasure in some cases, restriction of use, data portability and objection. A subject access request must be answered within one month. The ICO can issue fines. The higher maximum fine under the UK GDPR is £17.5 million or 4% of annual worldwide turnover, whichever is higher. Most problems are not caused by big failures but by everyday errors such as emailing the wrong person.

questions.prompt: What does the principle of purpose limitation mean?

options.text: Using data only for the purpose it was collected for
Keeping data for a limited time
Collecting as little data as possible
Sharing data only inside the department

questions.hint: Data collected for one reason should not be used in an incompatible way.

questions.prompt: What does storage limitation mean?

options.text: Keeping data in a locked cabinet
Limiting the number of files in a folder
Storing data only on departmental servers
Not keeping personal data longer than necessary

questions.hint: Data should be deleted when it is no longer needed.

questions.prompt: Which principle requires personal data to be kept secure?

options.text: Integrity and confidentiality
Lawfulness, fairness and transparency
Purpose limitation
Accuracy

questions.hint: Security is covered by the integrity and confidentiality principle.

questions.prompt: What does accountability mean in data protection?

options.text: You must be able to show that you follow the rules
You must name a person who is to blame for breaches
You must publish all data you hold
You must ask permission for every email you send

questions.hint: Organisations must demonstrate compliance.

questions.prompt: Which lawful basis do government departments most often rely on?

options.text: Legitimate interests
Public task
Contract
Consent

questions.hint: Public authorities often process data to carry out their official functions.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the six lawful bases?

options.text: Convenience for the organisation
A contract with the individual
Vital interests of an individual
Legal obligation placed on the organisation

questions.hint: Convenience is not a lawful basis.

options.text: Recording when staff have read a security policy
Listing the staff who can access a database

Asking customers to agree to receive adverts

questions.hint: A privacy notice supports the transparency principle.

questions.hint: Rectification relates to accuracy.

options.text: Twelve months
Three months
One month
Seven days

questions.hint: The standard time limit is one month.

items.title: Phishing and fraud: spotting and responding (Level 2)
items.source: NCSC guidance on phishing; GOV.UK security guidance
items.body: Most phishing is sent to thousands of people, but spear phishing is aimed at a particular person or team. The attacker may use your name, job title and details from social media to make the message look genuine. Attackers also pretend to be a senior manager asking for an urgent payment, a supplier sending a new invoice or a request to change bank details. Check the sender's address as well as the display name. Government email addresses end in gov.uk, for example name@dwp.gov.uk, whereas a lookalike such as name@dwp-gov.co could be fake. Fake login pages copy a real site. Type the address yourself or use a saved bookmark rather than following a link. Be careful with attachments, especially those that ask you to 'enable macros' or are an unexpected file type such as .exe. If a request involves money, passwords or changes to bank details, check it through another route, such as calling a number you already know, not one in the message. If you have clicked a link or opened an attachment by mistake, do not hide it. Tell your IT or security team straight away and change your password. Quick action limits the harm. Members of the public can report suspicious emails to the NCSC at report@phishing.gov.uk. Never read out a multi-factor authentication code to a caller. Unknown USB sticks should be handed to security, not plugged in.

questions.prompt: In cyber security, what is spear phishing?

options.text: Phishing that uses a spear-shaped logo
Phishing that targets everyone in a country
Phishing aimed at a particular person or team
Phishing sent only by text message

questions.hint: Spear phishing uses personal details to look convincing.

questions.prompt: Which sender address looks most suspicious for a message claiming to come from the DWP?

options.text: an address copied from the department's staff directory
name@dwp-gov.co
name@dwp.gov.uk with the correct display name
name@dwp.gov.uk

questions.hint: Genuine government addresses end in gov.uk; a lookalike domain is a warning sign.

questions.prompt: You click a link in a suspicious email by mistake. What should you do first?

options.text: Tell your IT or security team straight away
Close the browser and carry on with your work
Forward the email to your manager
Wait a day to see whether anything unusual happens

questions.hint: Quick reporting limits the damage.

questions.prompt: An email from a supplier asks you to change their bank details for the next payment. What is the safest step?

options.text: Call the number given in the email
Make the change and tell your manager afterwards
Reply to the email to ask if the request is genuine
Call the supplier on a number you already hold to check

questions.hint: Verify through a route you already trust, not one supplied in the message.

questions.prompt: Why is typing a web address or using a bookmark safer than clicking a link in an email?

options.text: The link may go to a fake page that copies the real one
Bookmarks are encrypted
Links in emails are always slower
Typing avoids using the internet

questions.hint: Fake sites can look the same as real ones.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible response to an attachment that asks you to 'enable macros'?

options.text: Save the file and open it at home
Enable them once and then disable them
Do not enable them and report the email
Enable them if the sender is a colleague

questions.hint: Requests to enable macros are a common way of delivering malware.

questions.prompt: Where can members of the public forward suspicious emails to the NCSC?

options.text: reports@security.ncsc.org
report@phishing.gov.uk
phishing@police.uk
suspicious@gov.uk

questions.hint: The NCSC runs the Suspicious Email Reporting Service at that address.

questions.prompt: A caller says they are from IT and asks you to read out the code sent to your phone. What should you do?

options.text: Read it out if they know your name
Refuse, because the code must never be shared

questions.hint: MFA codes should never be given to anyone.

items.title: Sending information safely and reporting loss (Level 2)
items.source: ICO guidance on personal data breaches; HMG Security Policy guidance
items.body: Before you send personal or sensitive information, ask whether the recipient needs it, whether you have the right address and whether you are using an approved method. Email auto-complete often suggests the wrong person with a similar name, so check each address before you press send. When sending to many people who should not see each other's details, use Bcc. If an attachment contains sensitive data, protect it with a password or encryption. Send the password by a different route, such as a phone call or text, never in the same email. Use only approved tools to share files, and do not use personal accounts or messaging apps for official business unless your department has approved them. Remember that hiding a column, row or sheet in a spreadsheet does not remove the data. It is still in the file. Delete it, or save a copy with only the needed information. In the same way, covering text with a black highlight in a document does not remove the text underneath. Use proper redaction tools that remove the content. If you lose a laptop, phone or paper files, or send something to the wrong person, report it to your line manager and the security or data protection team straight away. Do not wait to see if it turns up. Reporting near misses also helps the department to learn. Never leave devices or papers unattended in a car or public place.

questions.prompt: Why should the password for a protected attachment be sent by a different route?

options.text: Passwords are too long to put in an email
Email systems block attachments that mention a password
The recipient must be able to guess it first
If both arrive together, anyone who intercepts the email can open the file

questions.hint: Sending the password separately keeps the file protected.

questions.prompt: What risk does email auto-complete create?

options.text: It can change the language of the email
It can attach the wrong file
It can suggest the wrong person with a similar name
It can send the email without a subject

questions.hint: Always check the recipient's full address before sending.

questions.prompt: What happens to the data in a column that you hide before sharing a spreadsheet?

options.text: It stays in the file and the recipient can reveal it
It is kept but turns into plain text
It is removed from the file when you save it
It is moved to a protected area of the file

questions.hint: Hidden columns, rows and sheets can be revealed again by the recipient.

questions.prompt: Why is a black highlight not a safe way to hide text in a document?

options.text: Black highlight is not available in all versions
The text is still under it and can be copied
It changes the file size
It makes the document harder to print

questions.hint: Use a proper redaction tool that removes the underlying text.

questions.prompt: You have lost a work phone. What should you do?

options.text: Report it to your line manager and security team straight away
Report it only if it holds personal data
Buy a replacement and report it at the end of the month
Look for it for a day before reporting

questions.hint: Delay increases the risk of harm.

questions.prompt: When is it acceptable to use a personal messaging app for official business?

options.text: When you are working from home
When the recipient asks you to
When the message is short
Only when your department has approved it

questions.hint: Official information should use approved channels.

questions.prompt: Why should near misses be reported?

options.text: So that the person responsible can be disciplined
To avoid needing a privacy notice
The department can learn and prevent a real breach
Because the ICO must be told about all of them

questions.hint: Reporting near misses helps improve procedures.

options.text: Subject
Bcc
Cc
To

questions.hint: Bcc keeps recipients' addresses private from each other.
